lesson_title: The Mole: One Bag to Count the Invisible
hook_text: Chemists count things nobody can see — with a trick they stole from the rice depot.
clip_script: Picture the bulk depot where the corner shops stock up. Nobody at that counter counts grains of rice — grains are too small and far too many, so rice moves in bags, every bag identical, and the depot counts bags. Chemistry has the same problem, several sizes worse: no scale on Earth will ever weigh one molecule. So chemists fixed a bag size and counted bags. The bag is called the mole, and its size is six comma zero two times ten to the twenty-three particles — Avogadro's number. And the size was chosen to make the scale honest: one mole of anything weighs, in grams, exactly the number the periodic table prints for it. The periodic table is a price list, written in grams per bag. So when a camping canister leaks 8,8 grams of propane, you do not panic — you read the invoice. Three carbons, eight hydrogens: forty-four grams a bag. And 8,8 is one fifth of forty-four — a fifth of a bag, 0,2 moles, which is over a hundred thousand billion billion molecules, filling four and a half litres of air. Weighing became counting. That is the mole.
visual_style: A depot counter stacked with identical rice bags morphing into glowing molecular bags; a giant periodic table lights up as a price list; a propane canister leaks a shimmering cloud that condenses into the number 0,2 above a taxi rank labelled MOLES with three glowing routes out.
mood: Streetwise aha-moment — a huge abstract number made ordinary at a shop counter.
pacing: Relaxed depot open, quickening invoice arithmetic, big-number crescendo, calm one-line landing.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and make the mole map your reflex before exams.
